name: The two natures of the Lord (aparā and parā prakṛti)

definitions.definition: BhG 7.4–6: the Lord's prakṛti is twofold — the lower (aparā), divided eightfold into earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and I-making, and the higher (parā), which has become the living being (jīva-bhūtā) and upholds the world; all beings have these two as their womb, and the Lord is the origin and dissolution of the whole world.

name: The Lord's sovereign yoga (yogam aiśvaram): beings in him, he not in them

definitions.definition: BhG 9.4–6 (with 7.12): the world is pervaded by the Lord in his unmanifest form; all beings abide in him but he does not abide in them; and yet beings do not abide in him — 'behold my sovereign yoga': his self sustains and brings forth beings without abiding in them; as the great wind moving everywhere always abides in space, so all beings abide in him. At 7.12 the guṇa-states are said to be from him, he not in them, they in him.

BhG 7.16–19: four kinds of people of good deeds worship the Lord — the afflicted (ārta), the one who seeks to know (jijñāsu), the seeker of an object/wealth (arthārthin) and the knower (jñānin). All are noble, but the knower, ever yoked and devoted to the One, is distinguished: he is exceedingly dear to the Lord and the Lord to him, and is held to be the Lord's very self; at the end of many births he takes refuge knowing 'Vāsudeva is all' — a great soul very hard to find.

BhG 7.30; 8.5–7: whoever departs at the end remembering the Lord alone attains his state; whatever state one remembers when giving up the body, to that one goes, having always been shaped by it; therefore remember him at all times (and fight); those who know him together with adhibhūta, adhidaiva and adhiyajña know him even at departure.

BhG 8.9–13: at the time of departure the yogin, with unmoving mind, joined with devotion and the power of yoga, settles the breath between the brows and reaches the supreme divine Person; or, restraining all the gates, confining the mind in the heart, placing his breath in the head, established in yogic concentration, uttering Oṃ and remembering the Lord, he leaves the body and goes to the supreme goal.

name: The two paths after death (bright and dark)

definitions.definition: BhG 8.23–27: the two perennial courses of departing yogins — the bright (śukla): fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course, by which knowers of brahman go to brahman and do not return; and the dark (kṛṣṇa): smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern course, by which the yogin reaches the lunar light and returns. Knowing the two paths, the yogin is not deluded.

BhG 8.15–16, 8.21, 8.23–26; 9.3, 9.21: all worlds up to Brahmā's realm are subject to return; the Vedic sacrificers who reach heaven re-enter the mortal world when their merit is exhausted ('going and coming'); the faithless return to the path of death-and-wandering; but those who reach the Lord — his supreme abode, the imperishable unmanifest — do not come to rebirth, 'the impermanent home of suffering'; of the two paths of the departing, one leads to non-return, the other to return.

name: The three planes: divine, bodily, sacrificial

definitions.definition: BhG 7.29–30; 8.1–4: six terms to be known together with the Lord — brahman (the supreme imperishable), adhyātma (its own being, svabhāva), karma (the sending-forth that makes beings arise), adhibhūta (perishable being), adhidaiva(ta) (the Person, puruṣa), and adhiyajña (the Lord himself, here in the body); those who know him with these know him even at the time of departure.

name: The ages, the Manu-periods and the day of Brahmā

definitions.definition: BhG 8.17–19: the day of Brahmā extends to a thousand yugas and his night likewise; at the coming of day all manifest things arise from the unmanifest, and at the coming of night they dissolve into it; the same multitude of beings comes to be again and again, helplessly.

name: Kalpa, the day of Brahmā and his lifetime

definitions.definition: BhG 9.7–8: at the end of a kalpa all beings go into the Lord's prakṛti; at the beginning of a kalpa he, taking hold of his own prakṛti, sends forth again the whole multitude of beings, helpless under prakṛti's power.

BhG 7.24; 8.18–21; 9.4: manifest things come forth from and dissolve into the unmanifest with Brahmā's day and night; beyond that unmanifest is another, eternal unmanifest which does not perish when beings perish, called the akṣara, the highest goal and the Lord's supreme abode; the Lord pervades the world in unmanifest form; the unintelligent think him, the unmanifest, to have come into manifestation.

BhG 8.3, 8.11, 8.13, 8.20–21: brahman is the supreme imperishable; it is the akṣara of which the knowers of the Veda speak, which passionless ascetics enter and for which people practise brahmacarya; Oṃ is the one-syllable brahman; the eternal unmanifest beyond the unmanifest is called the akṣara, the highest goal, from which there is no return, the Lord's supreme abode.

BhG 7.14–15, 7.25: the Lord's divine māyā, made of the guṇas, is hard to cross; those who take refuge in him alone cross it; it carries off the knowledge of evil-doers; veiled by his yoga-māyā the Lord is not manifest to all.

BhG 7.12–14: the sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa states are from the Lord, yet he is not in them — they are in him; deluded by these three guṇa-made states the whole world does not recognise him who is beyond them; his divine māyā is made of the guṇas.

BhG 7.8–11 and 9.16–19 (the word vibhūti itself is not used in these verses): the Lord is the taste in water, the light of moon and sun, Oṃ in all the Vedas, sound in space, manhood in men, pure fragrance in earth, brilliance in fire, life in all beings, austerity in ascetics, the eternal seed of beings, the intelligence of the intelligent, the splendour of the splendid, strength free of desire and passion, desire not opposed to dharma; and the rite, the sacrifice, the offering, the fire and the oblation, father, mother, sustainer and grandfather of the world, Oṃ and the three Vedas, goal, witness, refuge and friend, immortality and death, sat and asat.

name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: BhG 7.15; 9.11–13: evil-doers who have resorted to a demonic disposition (āsura bhāva) do not take refuge in the Lord; those who disregard him in human form, of vain hopes, vain acts and vain knowledge, resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras; the great souls resort to the divine nature (daivī prakṛti) and worship him with undivided mind.

BhG 9.20–21: those versed in the three Vedas, soma-drinkers purified of sin, worship with sacrifices and pray for heaven; they reach the world of the lord of the gods and enjoy the gods' divine pleasures, but when their merit is exhausted they re-enter the world of mortals — 'going and coming'. 8.16: the worlds up to Brahmā's are subject to return.

BhG 7.21–22; 9.3, 9.23: whatever form a devotee wishes to worship with faith, the Lord makes that faith unwavering, and through it the worshipper obtains desires ordained by the Lord; those without faith in this dharma return to saṃsāra; devotees of other deities worship with faith, and so worship the Lord, but not according to rule.

BhG 9.15–16, 9.24, 9.26–27: some worship the Lord by the sacrifice of knowledge; he is the rite, the sacrifice, the ancestral offering, the herb, the mantra, the butter, the fire and the oblation; he is the enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices; a leaf, flower, fruit or water offered in devotion he accepts; every act, eating, oblation, gift and austerity is to be done as an offering to him.

BhG 9.11 with 7.24–25 (the word avatāra is not used): the deluded disregard the Lord who has taken on a human body, not knowing his supreme state as great lord of beings; he is unborn and imperishable, veiled by his yoga-māyā and not manifest to all.

BhG 9.1–3: the most secret knowledge together with vijñāna is declared to one who does not carp (anasūyu); it is the royal knowledge and royal secret; those without faith in this dharma do not reach the Lord.
BhG 7.8, 8.13, 9.17: the Lord is the praṇava in all the Vedas and the oṃkāra; Oṃ is the one-syllable brahman, to be uttered while remembering the Lord at departure, leading to the supreme goal.
BhG 9.9–10: the acts of sending forth beings do not bind the Lord, who sits as if indifferent, unattached to them; prakṛti gives birth to the moving and unmoving with him as overseer.

BhG 7.14, 7.19, 7.29; 9.32: those who take refuge in the Lord alone cross his guṇa-made māyā; the knower takes refuge after many births knowing 'Vāsudeva is all'; those who take refuge strive for release from old age and death; whoever takes refuge — even those of sinful birth, women, vaiśyas and śūdras — reaches the highest goal. Evil-doers of demonic disposition do not take refuge (7.15).
